title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot
openingText: Who that cares much to know the history of man, and how the mysterious mixture behaves under the varying experiments of Time, has not dwelt, at least briefly, on the life of Saint Theresa, has not smiled with some gentleness at the thought of the little girl walking forth one morning hand-in-hand with her still smaller brother, to go and seek martyrdom in the country of the Moors? Out they toddled from rugged Avila, wide-eyed and helpless-looking as two fawns, but with human hearts, already beating to a national idea; until domestic reality met them in the shape of uncles, and turned them back from their great resolve. That child-pilgrimage was a fit beginning. Theresa’s passionate, ideal nature demanded an epic life: what were many-volumed romances of chivalry and the social conquests of a brilliant girl to her? Her flame quickly burned up that light fuel; and, fed from within, soared after some illimitable satisfaction, some object which would never justify weariness, which would reconcile self-despair with the rapturous consciousness of life beyond self. She found her epos in the reform of a religious order.
about:
In an English provincial town on the threshold of political reform, Dorothea Brooke wants a life of useful devotion and Tertius Lydgate wants to change medicine. Their ambitions enter a web of marriages, inheritances, debts, professional rivalries, and neighbors’ opinions. Other lives continually interrupt and reshape their plans.

George Eliot follows several households at once, allowing a person who seems selfish or ridiculous in one scene to become understandable in another. The narrator asks readers to examine the distance between intention and action, sympathy and judgment, and the lives people imagine and those they can actually live.

whyItMatters.title: Seeing beyond one person’s story
whyItMatters.body: The novel repeatedly moves from one consciousness to another. A choice that looks obvious from outside becomes harder to judge when the hopes, fears, and pressures behind it come into view.

whyItMatters.title: Ambition meets dependence
whyItMatters.body: Scientific work, religious conviction, marriage, and practical reform all depend on other people. Money and reputation shape what characters can do, even when they believe their purposes are entirely their own.

whyItMatters.title: The value of ordinary care
whyItMatters.body: Alongside its large ambitions, the novel attends to work, loyalty, and acts of kindness that attract little notice. It asks how a life can matter without becoming publicly celebrated.

angleCards.title: Marriage and imagined futures
angleCards.text: Watch what each person expects marriage to provide, and what happens when the other person has a different story in mind.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the marriages and courtships, tracing how expectation, money, power, and sympathy shape intimacy.

angleCards.title: Who gets believed?
angleCards.text: Follow the movement from private knowledge to rumor and public judgment. Notice when the narrator knows more than the town.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track evidence, gossip, and reputation, distinguishing what characters know from what they infer or want to believe.

angleCards.title: Reform under pressure
angleCards.text: Read medical, political, and practical improvements together. Ask what helps a good intention become effective work.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how reform depends on expertise, funding, cooperation, and the reformer’s willingness to understand other people.

angleCards.title: Learning sympathy
angleCards.text: Notice when Eliot redirects attention towards someone you have dismissed. Test how understanding a motive changes judgment without erasing responsibility.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the narrator’s experiments in sympathy and ask how compassion can coexist with accountability.

cast.name: Dorothea Brooke
cast.description: Eager to devote her life to something worthwhile, Dorothea looks for a purpose larger than the comfortable future expected of her.

cast.name: Celia Brooke
cast.description: Practical and attentive to ordinary pleasures, Celia often sees what her sister’s ideals obscure.

cast.name: Edward Casaubon
cast.description: A clergyman absorbed in an ambitious scholarly project, Casaubon hopes to give his work lasting authority.

cast.name: Tertius Lydgate
cast.description: Lydgate brings scientific ambitions and plans for medical reform into a town where patronage and reputation shape professional life.

cast.name: Rosamond Vincy
cast.description: Accomplished and socially ambitious, Rosamond imagines a future of refinement beyond the limits of her familiar circle.

cast.name: Fred Vincy
cast.description: Affectionate but unreliable, Fred hopes luck and inheritance will spare him difficult decisions about work.

cast.name: Mary Garth
cast.description: Mary’s wit and self-respect make her unwilling to confuse affection with excuses for bad conduct.

cast.name: Caleb Garth
cast.description: Caleb values skilled work and honest dealings. His devotion to useful labor offers a different measure of success from money or status.

cast.name: Will Ladislaw
cast.description: Independent in outlook and uncertain of his vocation, Will resists the paths other people prescribe for him.

cast.name: Nicholas Bulstrode
cast.description: Bulstrode’s wealth supports local institutions, giving his religious convictions considerable public influence.

cast.name: Harriet Bulstrode
cast.description: Born into the Vincy family, Harriet combines social pride with warmth and loyalty.

cast.name: Camden Farebrother
cast.description: Humane and alert to his own weaknesses, Farebrother offers friendship without demanding that people be flawless.

cast.name: Sir James Chettam
cast.description: Well-meaning and attentive to practical improvements, Sir James takes an active interest in the Brooke sisters.
